newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Gold revaluation can help debt only - Lamfalussy.
newsitem.headline: Gold revaluation can help debt only - Lamfalussy.

text.p: European Monetary Institure president Alexandre Lamfalussy on Thursday declined to comment on Bonn's proposal to revalue the Bundesbank's gold reserves.
Lamfalussy said, however, that it was his personal view that one-off revaluations could only be used to cut debt, not the state deficit.

Asked if he believed the Bonn/Bundesbank gold row was damaging the prospects of economic and monetary union (EMU), he said, "I think we have to wait and see what is happening. I do not know yet the precise contents of the German government proposal."

He admitted the EMI has proposed a revaluation of reserves after the decision to set up the European central bank, the successor to the EMI, was taken. "What happens between now and then depends on national authorities."

"The real question is whatever happens in terms of revaluation, what to do with the proceeds and whether they should or should not contribute to the reduction of debt and/or a reduction of the deficit."
"My personal view is quite clear: I could imagine to use this as a means of reducing the external debt. I cannot imagine you can use it to reduce the current deficit."
"The substance remains this is a one-off move and one-off moves can be used to cut the debt." Lamfalussy was speaking as he went into a conference with Belgian bankers.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel has drawn sharp criticism from the Bundesbank over his plan to revalue Germany's gold and currency reserves.
The Bonn government, struggling to meet the Maastricht Treaty criteria on EMU, plans to transfer part of the gain resulting from the revaluation to redeem old debt.
The fiercely independent Bundesbank opposes making the payment before the planned 1999 start of monetary union because it believes such a move would undermine the credibility of the single currency.
